actions.justification: Critical first step in ADHF management to confirm volume overload (JVD, peripheral edema, pulmonary crackles) and guide diuretic therapy. Patient has classic signs of acute pulmonary edema.

Essential to determine if patient is 'warm and wet' (hypertensive ADHF - vasodilators indicated) vs 'cold and wet' (cardiogenic shock - inotropes needed). With BP 180/110, likely warm/hypertensive profile.

Hypertensive ADHF with pulmonary edema (BP 180/110, SpO2 82%) - IV nitroglycerin is first-line to rapidly reduce preload/afterload and relieve pulmonary congestion. High BP and hypoxia make this urgent.

IV furosemide is a cornerstone treatment for ADHF with pulmonary edema. This patient has severe respiratory distress with SpO2 82%, pink frothy sputum indicating pulmonary edema - IV diuretic will reduce preload and alleviate pulmonary congestion urgently.
Chest X-ray is essential to confirm pulmonary edema, assess cardiomegaly, and rule out alternative causes of dyspnea. Critical for guiding management in this ADHF presentation.
Basic metabolic panel needed to assess renal function and electrolytes (especially potassium) before and during diuresis, and to evaluate for contributing metabolic derangements.
BNP will confirm ADHF diagnosis and quantify severity of decompensation; useful for guiding ongoing treatment and prognostication in this HFrEF patient.
Troponin is essential to rule out acute MI as precipitant of this decompensation, especially given new severe presentation with tachycardia and hypertension.

Complex ADHF with HFrEF, poorly controlled hypertension, and atrial fibrillation causing severe decompensation (SpO2 82%) warrants urgent cardiology input for management optimization including rate control strategy and advanced therapies.

Patient has ADHF with HFrEF, severe hypoxia (SpO2 82%), elevated BP, and tachycardia. Bedside echocardiography is indicated to assess ventricular function, wall motion, and guide further management including potential inotrope use.

Despite initial diuresis and vasodilation, patient remains severely hypoxic (SpO2 82%) with tachycardia (HR 115) suggesting possible cardiogenic shock component or inadequate forward flow with HFrEF. Inotropic support should be considered if echo confirms low output state or cardiogenic shock.
Mandatory action: obtain focused history including precipitating factors, medication compliance, recent fluid/salt intake, and prior HF hospitalizations to guide management.
